explanation: Fires inside multi-token technical or jargon compound terms, especially in crypto, auth and software contexts (libp2[p], SegW[it], off[-chain], proof[ of] work, :token_credential, Authorization: bearer, tensorflow/core[/framework]). It also fires on patent boilerplate like 'by way[ of]'. Weak on ordinary function words. Strong activation needs a specialized, conventional multiword name or term.

Fires on the verb or infinitive slot right after a statement of intent or task setup ('are to [be] placed', 'I am [trying]', 'I [want] to', 'is [to] prove', 'asked to [prove]'). This is typical of math problems and Q&A questions. It also fires on a few code tokens after modifiers ('pub [fn]', 'static [const]'). Weak elsewhere.

A mixture. It fires on separators between items in a list or enumeration (the ':' in a MAC address, '(' / newline before the next multiple-choice option, printf(" before 'd.', the space before a number). It also fires on the word 'soil'/'earth' in environmental contexts, plus scattered code punctuation and verbs like driving or installed.

Fires on the first token of an uncommon or technical word, or of a proper noun, right after an article or determiner, mostly 'a' or 'the' (a[ not]-for-profit, a[ Devon] Rex, the[ With]lacoochee, a[ but]yl, a[ probabil]istic, the[ Wasser]stein, complete[ No]etherian). The token often starts a multi-token word. Ordinary common words after articles give weak activation.

Fires on word-piece tokens that start or continue rare technical words and names (ant-itubercular, pl-asminogen, Sab-er, O-ph-eltes, ri-bose). It also fires on tokens inside nested math or code expressions such as denominators, exponents and array indices (a^[2], 3[!], text[[0]]). Mixes subword fragments in jargon with operands inside formulas or brackets.

Fires on function words and punctuation near the start of a document or right after a title or heading, in the first sentence or two (commas in early lists, 'We [hope]', 'is [brought] to you', 'has become the [latest]'). Many top examples are early-position tokens in intros or lists. Content tokens deep in a document are weak.

No clear shared feature. It fires on mid-word or second-half tokens of compounds in scientific and biomedical text (carbon[ic] anhydrase, dro[plets], ret[rov]iral, estr[adi]ol, eff[lux]). It also fires on scattered tokens like 'towards [paying] it down', cookie[Value], and money-flow phrasing ('that [went] toward').

Fires on a subword token early in a name or word that is not common English: foreign words (Cyrillic 'пр[ив]ет'), proper names (R[ix]ensart, [Pri]yanka, [Per]vez, McG[ly]nn), tech names (Xe[La]TeX), and legal 'DEN'IED. Also on some code or legal boilerplate tokens. Roughly the start of a multi-piece rare word.

Fires on tokens that complete a named entity or fixed phrase in encyclopedic or news text: 'based [on]', 'born ... [in]' Budapest, '14th [District]', 'All-Century [Team]', 'Grand [Prix]', the last pieces of proper names (Chick-fil[-A], Saf[eway], Prime[ira]). Also a few code tokens. Broadly, predicting the end of a fixed multiword name or construction.

Mainly fires on statement-ending semicolons and newlines in code, mostly Java/Android import lines and statements ending with ';' or '();' followed by a newline. It also fires strongly on Russian auxiliary verbs 'быть' / 'будет' after modals ('может [быть]'). Small extras from other non-English text.

Fires most strongly on 'subject' in the PHP license header boilerplate 'This source file is [subject] to the ... License'. It also fires on mixed technical tokens: numerical-method terms (mesh made [finer], numerical [method]), operators in algebra problems ('k [-] q', 'b[)]'), indentation whitespace in code, and assorted nouns. Only the license case is sharp.

Fires on the first subword fragment of a word or name in non-English text (German, Portuguese, French, Romanian, Turkish) or of a rare proper name in English (Min-ke, Pal-oc-ci, Be-ale, Mon-mouthshire, Con-za). The token begins a multi-piece word whose continuation is not yet determined. Common English words are weak.

Fires on '.com' in CDN URLs inside HTML (bootstrapcdn[.com]), on vivid evaluative adjectives (bewildered, astonishing, hilarious, inexpensive), and on byte fragments of CJK / Devanagari / Vietnamese text. These are unrelated groups with no shared context.

Fires on tokens that complete a stock phrase or term: 'External [links]', 'described [by]' (taxonomy), 'named in honour [of]', 'full table [scan]', 'tissue micro[array]', 'next [generation]', 'poly[ethylene]'. Across all genres, it fires where the token is the highly predictable completion of a fixed collocation. Weak on loosely predictable function words.
